text: Lucile M. Jones, born in 1955, is an American seismologist and a trusted public voice for earthquake science and safety in California. Recognized as one of the foremost authorities on earthquakes, she is often referred to as "the Beyoncé of earthquakes" and is frequently consulted for information on recent seismic events. Currently a research associate at the Seismological Laboratory at Caltech and the founder and chief scientist of the Dr. Lucy Jones Center for Science and Society, Jones previously worked at the US Geological Survey (USGS) from 1985 to 2016, where she conducted research on foreshocks, seismotectonics, and hazard science to enhance societal resilience after natural disasters. She was part of the team that developed the Great Shakeout Earthquake Drills, which involve millions worldwide in annual safety drills. Jones has authored over 100 research papers focusing on the physics of earthquakes, foreshocks, hazard assessment, and the seismotectonics of southern California. She earned a Bachelor of Arts in Chinese language and literature, magna cum laude, from Brown University in 1976 and a Ph.D. in geophysics from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 1981. In February 1979, she visited China to study the 1975 Haicheng earthquake, becoming one of the first U.S. scientists to enter China after diplomatic relations normalized. She has served as past Secretary of the Seismology Section of the American Geophysical Union and past director and chair of the publications committee of the Seismological Society of America. Jones served as Science Advisor for Risk Reduction for the USGS Natural Hazards Mission Area under the SAFRR Project, as a Commissioner of the California Seismic Safety Commission (CSSC) appointed by Governor Gray Davis in 2002 and reappointed by Governor Arnold Schwarzenegger in 2005, and as a member of the California Earthquake Prediction Evaluation Council. In January 2014, she partnered with the USGS and the City of Los Angeles to serve as Seismic Risk Advisor to Mayor Eric Garcetti. After retiring from the USGS in 2016, she founded the Dr. Lucy Jones Center for Science and Society and published a book in 2018 titled The Big Ones: How Natural Disasters Have Shaped Us (and What We Can Do About Them), which examines major natural disasters like volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, floods, and hurricanes and analyzes human responses to understand future crisis survival. She was a resident at the University of Oregon's Wayne Morse Center for Law and Politics as the Wayne Morse Chair, where she delivered public talks on disaster preparedness and science communication. Since 1986, she has given numerous press interviews on significant southern California earthquakes, often in collaboration with fellow Caltech seismologist Kate Hutton. Tom Jordan of the Southern California Earthquake Center noted that Jones provides a calming and authoritative voice to the public during disasters and that her high public profile may make her one of the most effective chairs of the CSSC. Her reputation as a calm and reassuring figure stems in part from an incident after the 1992 Joshua Tree earthquake, when she answered press questions while holding her sleeping child; in a 2011 interview, she denied the claim that she asked the press to be quiet to avoid waking her son and expressed regret that she became a symbol of women achieving everything. In 2014, her presence at Los Angeles City Hall, supported by the USGS, contributed to the passage of a 2015 retrofitting plan that would improve seismic survivability for over 15,000 structures built with soft first stories and non-ductile concrete. Despite her focus on earthquakes, Jones has been called upon to comment on other crises, including the COVID-19 pandemic, advocating that the public be given "one clear message" to avoid confusion, such as "don't share your air" through mask-wearing and physical distancing. In 2022, she founded "Tempo: Music for Climate Action" to bring together climate scientists, social scientists, and musicians to explore climate issues. She has received the Alquist Award from the California Earthquake Safety Foundation, the Shoemaker Award for Lifetime Achievements in Science Communication from the USGS, the Samuel J. Heyman Service to America Medal from the Partnership for Public Service in 2015, and the Seismological Society of America's Frank Press Public Service Award in 2018. In 2024, Jones was named one of USA Today's Women of the Year. Her uncle was an American diplomat in Taiwan, and she lived with his family there; she graduated as salutatorian from the Taipei American School in 1971 before attending Brown University. A fourth-generation resident of southern California, Jones currently resides in Pasadena. She is married to fellow seismologist Egill Hauksson and has two sons. Jones is also a musician and composer who plays the viol, a Renaissance stringed instrument. She is a member of Los Angeles Baroque, known as "LA's Community Baroque Orchestra." In 2019, she released a music video for a piece titled In Nomine Terra Calens, which translates to "In the Name of a Warming Earth," a musical interpretation of global temperature data from 1880 to 2017 showing a "terrifying" rate of increase. The piece was performed by Los Angeles Baroque at the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County in February 2019. Her Chinese name is 章光月.
